title: Viruses
introduction: How can infectious particles with no ribosomes exploit cells, persist quietly and evolve so rapidly?
objectives: Compare capsid, genome and optional envelope
Explain lambda productive and lysogenic pathways
Interpret evidence for viral origins and rapid evolution

sections.guidingQuestion: How does a virion package heredity without being a cell?
sections.explanation:
Viruses are acellular infectious agents. A complete virion carries a nucleic-acid genome—DNA or RNA—protected by a protein capsid. It has no cytoplasm or ribosomes, and viral particles do not independently generate ATP or synthesize proteins. Many carry very few enzymes; a viral enzyme packaged in a particle is not evidence of self-sustaining cellular metabolism.

A capsid consists of repeating protein subunits that organize to protect the genome and help initiate infection. Virus particles typically have characteristic shapes and sizes, but their dimensions and biochemical capabilities vary greatly among lineages. Replication requires access to a living host cell's resources and machinery.

A purified bacteriophage remains a structured particle outside its host; once it infects a bacterium, the host's translation system produces phage proteins.

All viruses contain a nucleic-acid genome packaged with a protective protein capsid, although the genome may be DNA or RNA. Some viruses also have a lipid envelope acquired from a host membrane and bearing viral proteins. A capsid is assembled from protein subunits and protects the genome during transmission; it is not a cytoplasm. Viruses do not possess a complete ribosome-based protein-synthesis system, and a virion outside a host does not carry out autonomous metabolism or division. A labelled virus diagram should distinguish capsid from genome, and mark an envelope only for enveloped examples. These shared features explain dependence on cells while still allowing structural diversity.
sections.revisionSummary: Genome of DNA or RNA, protein capsid and lack of cytoplasm/ribosomes; not all have an envelope.
terms: Capsid: protein shell enclosing the viral genome

sections.guidingQuestion: Which structures differ among lambda phage, coronavirus and HIV?
sections.explanation:
Bacteriophage lambda is a tailed phage with a double-stranded DNA genome packaged in a head and a tail apparatus that delivers DNA into a suitable bacterium. Coronaviruses have a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome associated with a nucleocapsid and a lipid envelope bearing spike proteins. HIV is an enveloped retrovirus with two copies of positive-sense RNA and a characteristic cone-shaped capsid containing enzymes such as reverse transcriptase.

A viral envelope derives from host-cell membranes and contains viral proteins important for entry. Non-enveloped viruses rely on capsid surfaces for interactions with host cells. Genome chemistry, number of strands, shape and presence of envelope must be identified separately; an envelope does not imply that a virus is a cell.

A diagram showing protruding spikes and a lipid envelope may depict a coronavirus, but the presence of spikes alone is not enough to identify a species without additional information.

A bacteriophage such as lambda has a complex head-and-tail morphology; tobacco mosaic virus has an elongated helical arrangement; influenza and HIV are enveloped viruses with very different RNA genomes and replication mechanisms. Capsid shapes can be helical, icosahedral or more complex, and viral genetic material can be single- or double-stranded DNA or RNA. An envelope is optional and typically surrounds a capsid or other protein-associated genome structure. Avoid drawing every virus as a round spiked particle with an envelope. When analysing a micrograph, describe the visible morphology first and use genome type only if given by a label or additional evidence; it cannot reliably be read from shape alone.
sections.revisionSummary: Lambda: dsDNA, non-enveloped tailed phage; coronavirus: +ssRNA, enveloped; HIV: two +ssRNA copies, enveloped retrovirus.
terms: Envelope: host-derived lipid membrane containing viral proteins
Retrovirus: RNA virus using reverse transcription

sections.guidingQuestion: What sequence produces new lambda phage particles and destroys a host cell?
sections.explanation:
In the lytic pathway, lambda phage first adsorbs to specific receptors on Escherichia coli, then transfers its DNA into the bacterium. Viral genes redirect cellular transcription and translation, while the phage genome is replicated. Phage components assemble into new heads and tails and DNA is packaged.

Late viral gene products disrupt the bacterial envelope so progeny phages can leave. The infected bacterium supplies ATP, nucleotides, amino acids and ribosomes; the phage genome encodes instructions directing the process. The stages overlap biologically, although a staged diagram is useful for reasoning.

If host ribosome function is experimentally blocked after infection, new phage proteins cannot be produced even if viral DNA entered the bacterium.

In a lytic bacteriophage infection, attachment to a susceptible bacterial host is followed by delivery of the viral genome, expression of viral genes, copying of viral nucleic acid, production of capsid components and assembly of new phages. Phage proteins then damage the bacterial wall or membrane so the host lyses and releases virions. At each stage the virus uses host energy, ribosomes and metabolic resources; the phage does not grow into a larger phage or divide by binary fission. For lambda, this is one of two possible developmental pathways. Draw a sequence with arrows and identify the fate of both the host and the viral genome.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can lambda DNA be copied without immediate destruction of the bacterium?
sections.explanation:
A temperate lambda phage can establish lysogeny after entering E. coli. The phage DNA circularizes and can integrate into the bacterial chromosome as a prophage. Regulation of phage gene expression keeps lytic functions repressed while the bacterial cell grows and replicates.

During host division, the prophage is copied along with bacterial DNA and inherited by descendants. Certain stresses can induce the prophage to excise and enter the lytic programme. Lysogeny therefore changes the timing and vertical inheritance of the viral genome; it does not convert the virion into a self-sustaining organism.

A bacterium carrying integrated lambda DNA can produce generations of daughter cells without lysing; induction later can initiate phage production and lysis.

After lambda DNA enters an appropriate bacterial cell, it may integrate into the bacterial chromosome as a prophage. Host DNA replication then copies the integrated viral DNA into daughter cells as the bacterium divides. Viral regulatory genes normally repress production of lytic proteins, so the host can continue living rather than immediately rupturing. A stress response such as DNA damage can trigger induction, excision of the prophage and entry into lytic replication and eventual lysis. Lysogeny is not an indefinitely inactive virus outside a cell; it is a genome-maintenance relationship inside a reproducing host. Compare the long-term fate of the genome in the two pathways.

sections.guidingQuestion: What evidence challenges the idea of one ancestral virus lineage?
sections.explanation:
Virus genomes and replication systems are extraordinarily varied; viruses do not share a universal gene comparable to the conserved ribosomal genes of cellular organisms. Proposed evolutionary routes include escape of mobile genetic elements, reduction from more complex parasitic ancestors, and the long-term evolution of ancient replicators. Different groups may have histories involving different routes.

Viruses share the genetic code with cellular life and depend on cells, but those facts alone cannot establish a single viral origin. Similar traits, such as an obligately parasitic mode of existence, can arise convergently. Sequence homology in particular gene families is more informative about individual relationships than superficial resemblance among particles.

If two unrelated virus lineages both have envelopes, the envelope is not sufficient evidence that they descend from a single enveloped ancestor.

Viruses show striking differences in genome chemistry, replication enzymes, capsid structures and evolutionary histories. These differences have motivated hypotheses that some viruses arose from mobile genetic elements that escaped cells and others from lineages that became more dependent on hosts; distinct lineages could have different origins. Similarities between some virus genes and cellular genes provide clues, but reconstructing very ancient viral origins is difficult because viral sequences change rapidly and there is little direct fossil evidence. The evidence does not support one simple universal sequence of origin for all viruses. Scientific answers must distinguish phylogenetic observations from hypotheses about the historical process that generated them.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why can antiviral resistance and immune escape evolve quickly?
sections.explanation:
Many RNA viruses produce enormous numbers of descendants in short replication cycles, often with error-prone genome copying. This creates heritable variants on which selection can act. Influenza evolves through the accumulation of substitutions affecting antigenic proteins (antigenic drift); reassortment of RNA genome segments can also produce major combinations when compatible viruses coinfect a cell.

HIV undergoes rapid evolution through reverse-transcription errors, selection during infection and the immense size and turnover of its viral populations. Resistant variants can increase under drug pressure. Effective combination antiretroviral treatment lowers replication and reduces the probability that a lineage carries sufficient resistance mutations. A treatment does not deliberately cause adaptive mutations; it selects among existing and newly arising variants.

An influenza vaccine strain can become less well matched to later circulating strains as surface antigens diverge. HIV therapy typically targets several stages so one resistance change is less likely to defeat treatment.

Many RNA viruses produce large numbers of descendants and copy their genomes with relatively high error rates, generating variation on which selection can act. HIV evolves within and between hosts; changes can alter susceptibility to antiviral drugs and recognition by immune responses. Influenza viruses change through accumulated mutations in surface proteins (antigenic drift), and reassortment between segmented genomes can sometimes cause more abrupt combinations. The exact rate of change differs among viruses and genomic regions. A mutation is not directed toward better adaptation: beneficial variants may become more common under particular selective conditions. Explain why repeated vaccine assessment and drug-resistance surveillance are important consequences.
sections.revisionSummary: Drift involves accumulated sequence changes; reassortment exchanges influenza segments; HIV resistance reflects selection among variable viral genotypes.
terms: Antigenic drift: gradual antigen changes through mutations
Reassortment: exchange of genome segments in coinfected cells
sections.workedExample: An influenza vaccine strain can become less well matched to later circulating strains as surface antigens diverge. HIV therapy typically targets several stages so one resistance change is less likely to defeat treatment.

misconceptions.misconception: Antivirals instruct HIV to mutate specifically to survive.
misconceptions.correction: Mutation creates variants without foresight; antiviral selection changes their frequencies.

questions.prompt: Explain the mechanism and its consequence: How does a virion package heredity without being a cell?
questions.answer: Viruses are acellular infectious agents. A complete virion carries a nucleic-acid genome—DNA or RNA—protected by a protein capsid. It has no cytoplasm or ribosomes, and viral particles do not independently generate ATP or synthesize proteins. Many carry very few enzymes; a viral enzyme packaged in a particle is not evidence of self-sustaining cellular metabolism. A capsid consists of repeating protein subunits that organize to protect the genome and help initiate infection. Virus particles typically have characteristic shapes and sizes, but their dimensions and biochemical capabilities vary greatly among lineages. Replication requires access to a living host cell's resources and machinery.
markingPoints: A capsid consists of repeating protein subunits that organize to protect the genome and help initiate infection.

questions.prompt: Explain the mechanism and its consequence: Which structures differ among lambda phage, coronavirus and HIV?
questions.answer: Bacteriophage lambda is a tailed phage with a double-stranded DNA genome packaged in a head and a tail apparatus that delivers DNA into a suitable bacterium. Coronaviruses have a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome associated with a nucleocapsid and a lipid envelope bearing spike proteins. HIV is an enveloped retrovirus with two copies of positive-sense RNA and a characteristic cone-shaped capsid containing enzymes such as reverse transcriptase. A viral envelope derives from host-cell membranes and contains viral proteins important for entry. Non-enveloped viruses rely on capsid surfaces for interactions with host cells. Genome chemistry, number of strands, shape and presence of envelope must be identified separately; an envelope does not imply that a virus is a cell.
markingPoints: Bacteriophage lambda is a tailed phage with a double-stranded DNA genome packaged in a head and a tail apparatus that delivers DNA into a suitable bacterium.
A viral envelope derives from host-cell membranes and contains viral proteins important for entry.

questions.prompt: Explain the mechanism and its consequence: What sequence produces new lambda phage particles and destroys a host cell?
questions.answer: In the lytic pathway, lambda phage first adsorbs to specific receptors on Escherichia coli, then transfers its DNA into the bacterium. Viral genes redirect cellular transcription and translation, while the phage genome is replicated. Phage components assemble into new heads and tails and DNA is packaged. Late viral gene products disrupt the bacterial envelope so progeny phages can leave. The infected bacterium supplies ATP, nucleotides, amino acids and ribosomes; the phage genome encodes instructions directing the process. The stages overlap biologically, although a staged diagram is useful for reasoning.
markingPoints: In the lytic pathway, lambda phage first adsorbs to specific receptors on Escherichia coli, then transfers its DNA into the bacterium.

questions.prompt: Explain the mechanism and its consequence: How can lambda DNA be copied without immediate destruction of the bacterium?
questions.answer: A temperate lambda phage can establish lysogeny after entering E. coli. The phage DNA circularizes and can integrate into the bacterial chromosome as a prophage. Regulation of phage gene expression keeps lytic functions repressed while the bacterial cell grows and replicates. During host division, the prophage is copied along with bacterial DNA and inherited by descendants. Certain stresses can induce the prophage to excise and enter the lytic programme. Lysogeny therefore changes the timing and vertical inheritance of the viral genome; it does not convert the virion into a self-sustaining organism.

questions.prompt: Explain the mechanism and its consequence: What evidence challenges the idea of one ancestral virus lineage?
questions.answer: Virus genomes and replication systems are extraordinarily varied; viruses do not share a universal gene comparable to the conserved ribosomal genes of cellular organisms. Proposed evolutionary routes include escape of mobile genetic elements, reduction from more complex parasitic ancestors, and the long-term evolution of ancient replicators. Different groups may have histories involving different routes. Viruses share the genetic code with cellular life and depend on cells, but those facts alone cannot establish a single viral origin. Similar traits, such as an obligately parasitic mode of existence, can arise convergently. Sequence homology in particular gene families is more informative about individual relationships than superficial resemblance among particles.
